clips.text_zh: BTC幾個星期唔郁 大家當佢死 然後一pump 15%就全衝入去 點解永遠係up咗先買? 我自己都係咁 廢柴。🙏
clips.text_en_b1: Why does everyone buy BTC after the pump? You watch BTC do nothing for weeks and ignore it completely. Then it pumps 15 percent and suddenly everyone wants in. This came up on /biz/ today and it hit me hard. I did the same thing last time too.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ thread on buying BTC after the move

signal.rationale: Post-hoc observation about FOMO, no actionable setup

clips.text_en_b2: Why is it that everyone piles into BTC only after it has already rallied? I sat watching it do absolutely nothing for weeks on end and basically ignored it. The moment it pumped fifteen percent, however, /biz/ exploded and the FOMO came rushing back. I fell for it last time as well, and honestly, that pattern is getting embarrassing at this point.
clips.text_en_c1: There is a perennial pattern in retail crypto behaviour that never ceases to baffle me: an asset flatlines for weeks, the consensus deems it dead, and the moment it rallies fifteen percent, the very same people who dismissed it rush in headlong. A thread on /biz/ crystallised this phenomenon today, and the cognitive dissonance was almost painful. I ought to feel above such impulses, yet I capitulated identically during the previous cycle. It seems the fear of missing out will reliably override any semblance of strategic patience, regardless of how many times one has sworn off chasing green candles.
clips.text_en_c2: There is a perennial irony embedded in retail crypto behaviour, one so consistent it borders on pathological. Bitcoin invariably languishes in prolonged lateral consolidation for weeks on end, during which period the broader investing public effectively writes it off as moribund; then, the moment it embarks on a sudden fifteen per cent upward surge, the very same cohort clamours to enter positions at precisely the worst possible juncture. A thread on /biz/ surfaced today crystallising this phenomenon, and the resultant self-reflection proved almost physically uncomfortable to read. Yours truly, I confess with no small measure of mortification, replicated the identical error during the previous cycle. The asymmetry between prescience and hindsight remains, as ever, brutally unforgiving. Cease buying tops, you imbeciles.

clips.text_zh: X Corp連環發cease and desist 連Nitter呢啲FOSS front-end都要告 仲要搞TwitterWebViewer呢啲embed仔 結果一堆alternative即刻起返晒。Musk正仆街lol。🧐
clips.text_en_b1: X Corp sent cease and desist letters to the Nitter project, claiming it violated the Texas Harmful Access by Computer Act and the Lanham Act. They went after individual instances and even unrelated embed sites like TwitterWebViewer. All complied because nobody wants to be sued. A dozen alternate front-ends popped up immediately.
clips.source_hint: /g/ thread on X Corp killing Nitter front-ends

signal.rationale: X platform drama is noise for the stock, no clear direction

clips.text_en_b2: X Corp has been firing off cease and desist letters left and right, going after the Nitter project, individual instances, and even unrelated embed sites such as TwitterWebViewer. They cited the Texas Harmful Access by Computer Act and the Lanham Act as justification. Everything complied almost immediately because nobody wants to get dragged into court, although a dozen alternative front-ends sprang up in response. Classic Musk overreach.
clips.text_en_c1: X Corp has escalated its legal offensive with a barrage of cease and desist letters, targeting the Nitter project under the Texas Harmful Access by Computer Act and the Lanham Act. Notably, the campaign extended beyond individual front-end instances to encompass entirely unrelated embed services such as TwitterWebViewer, presumably to establish broader precedent. Predictably, every operator complied, since few possess the resources to litigate against Musk's legal apparatus. The irony, of course, is that within hours a dozen alternative front-ends materialised, underscoring the futility of attempting to suppress decentralised infrastructure through conventional litigation. Musk remains, by any reasonable metric, a liability.
clips.text_en_c2: X Corp's latest legal offensive, an unrelenting barrage of cease and desist correspondence, has now extended its reach beyond the ostensibly obvious targets to encompass the Nitter project, a venerable FOSS front-end long cherished by those seeking to circumvent the platform's increasingly hostile architecture. The litigants have further cast their net absurdly wide, pursuing not merely primary instances but even peripheral embed utilities such as TwitterWebViewer, whose sole sin appears to be tangential association. Predictably, every recipient capitulated forthwith; nobody relishes a federal lawsuit. Yet the law of unintended consequences operates with characteristic vigour: within hours, a dozen fresh alternative front-ends materialised organically, a hydra-like proliferation that arguably renders the entire campaign counter-productive. Musk, you irredeemable clown. The Streisand effect, it transpires, remains undefeated.

clips.text_zh: 30年前日本同美國head2head 而家係G7最廢 仲係跌緊。人哋AI bubble起碼有tech 日本連債都借爛都冇tech。中國油元掛鈎嗰邊條post更加癲 wtf。
clips.text_en_b1: Japan has lost all of its high tech industries. Thirty years ago it was competing head to head with America in every technological field. Today it is probably the least advanced G7 nation and is still falling behind. At least the AI bubble and high end manufacturing overcapacity have the tech, even if the debt was insane.
clips.source_hint: /pol/ thread on Japan losing its tech edge

signal.rationale: Geopolitical commentary, not a trade setup

clips.text_en_b2: Japan has essentially squandered every high tech industry it once commanded. Thirty years ago it was going head to head with America across virtually every technological field, whereas today it ranks as probably the weakest G7 nation and keeps slipping further behind. Sure, the AI bubble and overcapacity stories come with plenty of red flags, but at least those economies still have the underlying tech. Japan, saddled with crushing debt, has nothing comparable to show for it.
clips.text_en_c1: Japan's technological decline over the past three decades represents one of the more striking reversals in modern economic history. Once a peer competitor to the United States across virtually every high-tech sector, the nation has now descended to what many consider the least innovative position within the G7, with the trajectory showing no meaningful reversal. While the American AI bubble and Chinese overcapacity narratives carry their own contradictions, they at least rest upon substantive technological foundations. Japan, by contrast, appears to be propping up fiscal accounts through ever-increasing debt issuance whilst haemorrhaging industrial relevance. The prognosis is, frankly, grim.
clips.text_en_c2: Japan's precipitous decline from technological pre-eminence constitutes, perhaps, the most underappreciated geopolitical story of the past three decades. At the close of the Cold War era, Japanese industry stood head-to-head with American counterparts across virtually every strategic sector, from consumer goods and semiconductors alike; today, by virtually any meaningful metric, it ranks as the least technologically dynamic member of the G7, and the trajectory continues inexorably downward. The American AI bubble, whatever its manifold excesses, is at least predicated upon genuine technological innovation and a manufacturing capacity that, debt-laden though it may be, retains substantive foundations. Japan, by contrast, has mortgaged its future through debt financing of biblical proportions whilst generating precisely nothing of comparable technological merit. A separate post concerning Chinese petroyuan arrangements borders on the genuinely unhinged.

clips.text_zh: Alpöge同Buckmaster用Claude同GPT解緊數學難題 OpenAI話佲嘅agent swarm自己搞掂 '不能排除'用咗人哋data 數學家冇credit 真係偷師。AI真係會搶job 工程佬小心。
clips.text_en_b1: Mathematicians Alpöge and Buckmaster were working on a hard problem using Claude and GPT. OpenAI then claimed an agent swarm solved it independently. Their statement said they could not rule out that de-identified data from the mathematicians helped. The mathematicians got no credit in the paper.
clips.source_hint: /g/ thread on OpenAI allegedly stealing a math breakthrough

signal.rationale: AI ethics story, not a trade

clips.text_en_b2: Mathematicians Alpöge and Buckmaster had reportedly been working through a notoriously difficult problem using Claude and GPT, and then OpenAI stepped in claiming an agent swarm cracked it independently. Their statement conceded they could not rule out that de-identified data from the original mathematicians had contributed to the result. Despite that, the paper offered those mathematicians zero credit, which has fuelled accusations straight across academic circles.
clips.text_en_c1: The mathematicians Alpöge and Buckmaster had been leveraging Claude and GPT to grapple with a particularly intractable problem when OpenAI announced that its agent swarm had resolved the same question independently. The company's carefully worded statement conceded that exposure to de-identified data from the researchers could not be ruled out, a hedge that essentially confirms what many already suspected. The mathematicians received no acknowledgement in the subsequent paper, prompting accusations of intellectual appropriation. This incident encapsulates broader anxieties regarding how large language models may quietly appropriate human expertise whilst rendering its originators redundant, a development that should concern any engineer whose work is reproducible.
clips.text_en_c2: A controversy of considerable methodological significance has emerged within mathematical circles, one that strikes at the foundational ethics of contemporary AI research. The mathematicians Alpöge and Buckmaster had been labouring assiduously upon a notoriously intractable problem, employing Claude and GPT as auxiliary tools throughout their investigative process. OpenAI subsequently announced that their agent swarm had achieved independent resolution of the identical problem, a claim that, whilst technically defensible, carried a rather conspicuous asterisk: their official statement conceded they could not categorically exclude the possibility that de-identified outputs from the human mathematicians had inadvertently seeded the training corpus. The original researchers, meanwhile, received no acknowledgement whatsoever in the published paper, a glaring omission that constitutes, by any reasonable standard, intellectual larceny of the first order.

clips.text_zh: /a/又戰緊動漫女角色嘅胸圍幾大先算too big 廢柴話題但係一班男人可以傾兩百層。我寧願睇Gundam 00。🧐
clips.text_en_b1: On /a/ today they were asking the classic question: when it comes to anime and manga busts, how big is too big? Hundreds of replies arguing about it. Some say it ruins the character design. Others say it is part of the appeal. The thread is still going as of tonight.
clips.text_en_b2: On /a/ today someone resurrected the timeless anime debate: how far is too far when it comes to bust sizes in character designs? It is a fairly pointless argument on paper, yet hundreds of replies have piled in, with some insisting it ruins the aesthetic and others arguing it is precisely the appeal. The thread kept on rolling well into the night without any sign of resolution.
clips.text_en_c1: The eternal question resurfaced on /a/ today: at what point do anime and manga bust sizes cross the threshold from appealing exaggeration into comedic absurdity? What began as a lighthearted inquiry metastasised into a two-hundred-post marathon, with factions entrenched on both sides. Purists contend that egregious proportions undermine character design and narrative credibility, whilst enthusiasts maintain that stylisation is integral to the medium's aesthetic vocabulary. The thread remained active well into the evening, demonstrating that ostensibly trivial cultural debates possess a remarkable capacity to sustain engagement indefinitely. One might more productively rewatch Gundam 00.
clips.text_en_c2: The venerable boards of /a/ have, once again, descended into their preferred locus of internecine warfare, a debate so magnificently puerile yet so irresistibly compulsive that it sustains itself indefinitely. The question, posed with the gravity of philosophical inquiry, concerns the precise threshold beyond which the anatomical proportions of fictional female characters transgress the boundaries of aesthetic plausibility and become, by universal consensus, excessive. Hundreds of replies have proliferate across two hundred plus distinct contributions, each dissecting the matter with the analytical rigour ordinarily reserved for questions of metaphysics. Some contend such proportions irrevocably compromise the integrity of character design, rendering figures grotesque and absurd; others argue, with equal conviction, that generous proportions constitute an integral element of the medium's distinctive appeal.

clips.text_zh: /fit/有廢話squat係meme lift 話古希臘人都唔做squat 淨係跑同揼重嘢 推bench OHP DL加跑步就夠。肥仔信聽到實笑 我自己都覺有啲道理但又唔想認。
clips.text_en_b1: An anon on /fit/ argued that squats are a meme lift prioritized way too much in modern training. He pointed out the ancient Greeks never did squats. They just ran and carried heavy things. His program is bench, OHP, deadlift, running, and farmer carries only.
clips.text_en_b2: One anon on /fit/ laid out a hot take claiming that squats are an overhyped meme lift that gets prioritised far too much in modern training programmes. His reasoning was that the ancient Greeks never bothered with them and simply ran or carried heavy loads instead. His proposed routine is bench, overhead press, deadlifts, running, and farmer carries. Skinnyfat guys are lapping it up, and I hate that the logic actually holds.
clips.text_en_c1: An anonymous poster on /fit/ mounted a contrarian argument that the squat has been elevated to an almost mythological status within contemporary strength training, far exceeding its actual utility. His evidence, somewhat dubiously, invoked the ancient Greeks, who apparently eschewed the movement entirely in favour of running and loaded carries. His proposed programme distils training to bench press, overhead press, deadlifts, running, and farmer carries, omitting any dedicated lower-body compound work. Skinnyfat novices will doubtless seize upon this as justification for skipping leg day, though I confess the logic, however flawed, carries a certain seductive appeal that I am reluctant to endorse openly.
clips.text_en_c2: A /fit/ regular has promulgated a heretical thesis that, however provocative, merits genuine consideration rather than reflexive dismissal: the squat, that vaunted cornerstone of contemporary strength training, may be considerably overrated, an artefact of modern gymnasium culture rather than a timeless movement pattern. His argument rests upon a curious empirical foundation, namely that the ancient Greeks, those paragons of physical development, never performed squats in any structured sense; their conditioning derived instead from sustained running and the carrying of ponderous implements across considerable distances. His resultant programme is austere in its economy: bench press, overhead press, deadlift, running, and farmer carries, with not a single knee bend in sight.

clips.text_en_c2: The Kingdom Hearts 4 rumour mill, already operating at fever pitch, has received yet another adrenaline shot courtesy of an achievement list unearthed on SteamDB this evening, a discovery that effectively confirms what eager fans had long speculated. The leaked content delineates an audacious roster that reads like a corporate wishlist come to fruition: Star Wars, Haunted Mansion, the Hundred Acre Wood, Zootopia, and an intriguing locale designated merely as Imagineer Planet, each entry suggesting Disney's full commercial weight has been deployed behind the project. Two further concealed achievements contain references that have set the speculation forums ablaze, one invoking a dark avenger figure, another a designation that, upon translation, yields something approximating emptiness or void. Season fifteen of any major television property could scarcely aspire to such a concentrated payload of corroborative data.
